paras: The Pacific Avenue police shooting took place in Dallas, Texas, at about 1 a.m. on August 1, 1890, when Officer Ragland of the city police chased an unnamed Black man from beneath a shed on Pacific avenue and fired five shots at him as he ran. The man outran the officer and escaped, and no wound was reported. The only known account, a Dallas special to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, told the shooting as a comic item in a column on petty theft.
The dispatch opened with a run of small thefts in Dallas, including a set of harness taken from city tax collector J. C. Bogie the same night, and with police warnings about "suspicious persons."

Officer Ragland found the man in what the paper called "his lair beneath a shed at Brady's hide house" on Pacific avenue. According to the dispatch, the man had a loaded six-shooter and a sack holding a beaded buckskin outfit of leggings, moccasins and a hunting pouch. While the officer was looking over these "trophies," the man slipped around the shed, and the officer followed and "fired the first shot from the negro's pistol," then fired five times in all while chasing him down the avenue. The man got away in the moonlight, and the officer went back for the sack, which was put on display at the city jail that morning.
The dispatch named no charge against the man, and no later report of his arrest, identity or any wound was found.

The Fort Worth Daily Gazette ran the item on page 7 on August 2 under the headings "Thieves Abroad" and "A Fleet Footed Negro Not Afraid of Bullets." Its tone was jocular: it called the man "the darky" and the officer's "game," and said the officer "stood no show in a foot race." The account came entirely from the police side, and no other white paper or Black newspaper was found to have reported the shooting.

quotes: About 1 o'clock this morning Officer Ragland chased a negro from his lair beneath a shed at Brady's hide house on Pacific avenue.
The officer followed and fired the first shot from the negro's pistol. The officer fired five times while chasing the fleeing fugitive down the avenue.
The officer stood no show in a foot race and his game was soon lost in the mellow moonlight.
